'''Jeremy Bernstein''' (December 31, 1929 – April 20, 2025) was an American [[theoretical physicist]] and popular science writer.

==Early life==
Bernstein's parents, Philip S. Bernstein, a [[Reform Judaism|Reform]] rabbi, and Sophie Rubin Bernstein named him after the biblical [[Jeremiah]], the subject of his father's [[Masters Thesis|masters thesis]].  Philip's parents were immigrants from [[Lithuania]], while Sophie was of Russian-Jewish descent.  The family moved from [[Rochester, New York|Rochester]] to [[New York City]] during [[World War II]], when his father became head of all the Jewish [[Chaplain|chaplains]] in the [[United States Armed Forces|armed forces]].<ref>Jeremy Bernstein, Personal History, [http://www.newyorker.com/archive/1987/01/26/1987_01_26_035_TNY_CARDS_000345766 “I-THE LIFE IT BRINGS,”] The New Yorker, January 26, 1987, p. 35</ref>

==Education and career==
Bernstein studied at [[Harvard University]], receiving his [[bachelor's degree]] in 1951, his [[Master's degree|master's]] in 1953, and his [[Ph.D.]] in 1955. His thesis research, on electromagnetic properties of [[deuterium]], was supervised by [[Julian Schwinger]].  As a theoretical physicist, he worked on elementary [[particle physics]] and [[cosmology]].  A summer spent in [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos]] led to a position at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]].<ref>Jeremy Bernstein, Personal History, [http://www.newyorker.com/archive/1987/02/02/1987_02_02_039_TNY_CARDS_000345957 “II-THE LIFE IT BRINGS,”] The New Yorker, February 2, 1987, p. 39</ref> In 1962 he became a faculty member at [[New York University]], moving to become a professor of [[physics]] at [[Stevens Institute of Technology]] in 1967, a position that he continued to hold after retirement as [[professor emeritus]].<ref name="brit">[http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/62638/Jeremy-Bernstein "Jeremy Bernstein,"] Encyclopædia Britannica</ref>  He has held [[Adjunct professor|adjunct]] or visiting positions at the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]], [[CERN]], [[Oxford]], the [[University of Islamabad]], and the [[Ecole Polytechnique]].<ref name="edge">[http://www.edge.org/memberbio/jeremy_bernstein "Jeremy Bernstein (member bio)"] at Edge.org</ref>

Bernstein was involved in [[Project Orion (nuclear propulsion)|Project Orion]], investigating the potential for [[nuclear pulse propulsion]] for use in [[Spaceflight|space travel]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bernstein |first=Jeremy |date=2020-05-04 |title=Reflections on Project Orion |url=https://inference-review.com/article/reflections-on-project-orion |journal=Inference |language=en |volume=5 |issue=2}}</ref> In 2025, before his death in April, he was the last living member of the senior personnel of the project.

Bernstein died on April 20, 2025, at the age of 95.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jeremy Bernstein |url=https://aspenphys.org/people/jeremy-bernstein/ |access-date=2025-08-16 |website=Aspen Center for Physics |language=en}}</ref>

==Popular writing==
Bernstein was a popular science writer and profiler of scientists. He was a staff writer for ''[[The New Yorker]]'' from 1961 to 1995, authoring scores of articles.<ref>The New Yorker, [http://www.newyorker.com/magazine/bios/jeremy_bernstein/search?contributorName=Jeremy+Bernstein Search:Jeremy Bernstein]</ref> He also wrote regularly for [[The Atlantic|''The Atlantic Monthly'']], the ''[[New York Review of Books]]'', and ''[[Scientific American]]'', among others. Bernstein's biographical profiles of physicists, including [[Robert Oppenheimer]], [[Hans Bethe]], [[Albert Einstein]], [[John Stewart Bell]] and others, were able to draw on the experiences of personal acquaintance.<ref name="brit" /><ref name="edge" /> In 2018, Bernstein published ''A Bouquet of Dyson: and Other Reflections on Science and Scientists.''<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 2018 |title=A Bouquet of Dyson: and Other Reflections on Science and Scientists |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/worldscibooks/10.1142/10762 |access-date=November 7, 2024 |website=World Scientific}}</ref>
